utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. We -- I would like to raise two matters before the witness is being brought in. We dealt yesterday again with the exhibits in relation to Witness Haglund and we received the information that four documents are still pending with the translation. The others will be admitted. And the understanding of the Chamber was that the parties agreed on those that don't need a translation. The Registry will provide and will circulate a memo with the P numbers for all these documents admitted into evidence. The other matter is, we left off yesterday in private session. I would like to indicate for the record that we had our hearing until 7.00 exactly and it was my mistake not to turn back into open session before we left. We have two days of hearings this week ahead, today and tomorrow. There are -- we have to finish this current witness quite soon, hopefully in the first session today, then there are two other witnesses scheduled and Dr. Brunborg to finish his testimony of last week. I would invite the parties, with every witness, to focus on the issues they are called for and not to waste time with other matters. I think there's a reason to mention that after the experience of this week with the current witness; both parties used lots of time with matters related to 1992 and 1993, but the witness was called for events in 1995. Therefore, I would like to invite the parties to look at the time and to see how to finish as soon as possible. Is Mr. Haglund [sic] still scheduled by the Prosecution for this week, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Yes, he is, and that's Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, I mixed the names up again; it's a shame, of course. I was referring to Mr. Brunborg. This is one more reason to hurry up as much as possible. The witness shall be brought in, please. We turn into closed session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope very much that we can finish your testimony quite soon. And I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me say some words. I think it's a very difficult situation for you here in the courtroom. If I interrupt you to have a pause between question and answer, this is nothing which is directed against you. This happens to everybody in the courtroom. Sometimes the Prosecutor doesn't pause, sometimes Mr. Tolimir doesn't pause. This is a problem, but it is not an action against you. If I cut you and ask you to wait. Don't worry about that, please. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. Peace in this house. I would like to say hello to all those present. I would like for this day of trial, as well as the entire trial, to end according to God's will and not according to mine. Yesterday we were looking at document 1D584. Could we see that in e-court, please. 1D584.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quoting what the document says, so can we look at the document. Now we can see the document. Once it is enlarged, we can read it. I'm going to read it; there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me first say that this is a document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Zepa Light Brigade sent on the 17th of January, 1995, to the General Staff of the army, to Kakanj, for Enver Hadzihasanovic personally. It was signed by the commander, Colonel Avdo Palic. Last time, we were talking about why there was no signature. All the Zepa documents were sent by electronic means and this is a document that was received by the OTP from the Bosnian authorities. And if documents are sent electronically, then they do not have an actual signature. I quote. First paragraph of this document: "I take this opportunity to send you my greetings and to remind you that on the 27th of January, 1995, the 1st Zepa Brigade will be celebrating its second anniversary. The 1st Zepa Brigade was formed on the 27th of January, 1993, emerging from the Patriotic League through the Territorial Defence units and the local communes of Zepa, Podrepje [phoen], Godjenje, and Luke, and the 4th Detachment and the 1st Zepa Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please slow down while reading. If you want to have it on the record, then you should slow down. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So I'm repeating a part of what I'm reading out. "From the Territorial Defence units --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat something. Just slow down. And continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... and the 4th June detachment and the 1st Zepa Detachment and the Zepa brigade was formed on the 27th of January, 1993." My question is: This document by Avdo Palic to the command of the General Staff of the B&H army, does it indicate that the 1st Zepa Brigade was formed on the 1st of January, 1993 -- on the 27th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it states in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we redact the name of the location from the transcript so that I can put my next question to the witness. Can we now look at 1D364, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, the document was dated 17th of January, 1995, if I'm not mistaken, and not 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a part of the transcript, and this document in this respect should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document so that I could call up the next document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment on this document. The dates here, the 27th of January, 1995, in the date, and then in the first paragraph there is the 27th of January, 1993, so I don't know which of these dates is correct. There's also no signature by Avdo Palic on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I'm just going to read the first sentence to you. "I take the opportunity to send you my greetings and to remind you that on the 27th of January, 1995, the 1st Zepa Brigade will be celebrating its second anniversary." So this was written on the occasion of the anniversary, and this is perhaps the reason why these dates are overlapping or -- or they correspond to each other.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is fine. The dates are the same. I don't know what I'm supposed to confirm with this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What did Avdo Palic -- I mean, did Avdo Palic write this document, and was this Zepa unit formed on the 27th of January, 1993; was he writing on the second anniversary of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note the last two, three questions and answers we were unable to interpret because the speakers are fast and overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped you Mr. Tolimir. We have the same trouble as yesterday. You should pause as well. And you are familiar with the proceedings here in the courtroom. The witness is not. Please pause. I think I made a mistake, I mixed up the dates 1993 and 1995. It's -- it was clear on the record. I agree to that. Now, you see, the interpreters had a problem to interpret everything what you were asking. So can you put a short question to the witness again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if the mail from the Zepa Brigade command going to this address from Sarajevo to Kakanj where it was sent by courier, did it arrive there by courier or was it sent electronically?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It something is sent as a telegram by teleprinter, are you aware that it cannot be signed by the person sending it? So, do you know if the outgoing telegram can bear the personal signature and can this signature be transmitted to the location where it is being sent?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand how teleprinters work. I don't understand these telegram/telegraph procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document that was sent by Avdo Palic into evidence so that we can move to the next question in order not to waste any more time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to ask the witness: Are you familiar with this celebration, the second celebration -- second anniversary celebration of this 1st Zepa Brigade? Do you recall anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a celebration, but it wasn't any kind of military fête. It was just a traditional celebration that is held every year. It usually took place in September. You would have some horse races, some sports competitions, soccer, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the first sentence, that on the 17th -- the 27th of January, 1995, the 1st Zepa Brigade will be celebrating its second anniversary; do you know anything about that? You were now referring to celebrations in September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. I don't know about this date. I don't know of any celebration being held then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may ask further questions to the content of this document, otherwise we -- at the moment we don't see a connection or we have some doubt if there is -- if this is the right witness to comment on this document. Perhaps you can establish some more by -- of the content by asking additional questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You answered a little bit earlier that your birth place, which is mentioned here but it was redacted from the transcript, and can you please tell us the unit from that birth place of yours that is referred to in the telegram went into the composition of the Zepa Brigade as Avdo Palic says in this telegram here?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I really don't know. I wasn't in the army at that time. This is why I don't know anything about this data here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know that you don't know, but was the Zepa Brigade formed on the 27th of January, 1993, as Mr. Palic says? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I don't want to waste any more time on this because you don't know anything about that, so let it be like that. Well, let's go on. We don't have any more time, so let's go on with the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D364, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document by Sead Delic, talking about successful sabotage actions by the Zepa Brigade against the Army of Republika Srpska. Yes, we can see the document now. This is the brigade commander, Sead Delic; he was the commander of the Tuzla Corps. He sent this to the command of the 28th Division, which was in Srebrenica, and to the command of the 285th Light Infantry Brigade. This was sent on the 28th of June. This was a full month before you actually left Zepa. He says the following, I quote. Paragraph 1: "I congratulate you on successfully carried-out combat whereby you have significantly contributed to the more successful execution of the operation to unblock Sarajevo and have inflicted heavy losses on the aggressor forces in the fight for the final liberation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the elimination of Serbo-Montenegrin Fascism."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which states: "Due to problems with the entry of the convoy to Zepa and Srebrenica, it is important at this point in time to have developed combat plans but to wait for more favourable time because of the difficult situation with food for the inhabitants and members of the B&H army and the MUP for further combat actions outside of the Srebrenica and Zepa zones." My question to you is this: Did the corps commander, Sead Delic, here congratulate the forces for the successful execution of operations and/or eliminating Serbo-Montenegrin Fascism?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if the humanitarian aid convoys were ever halted during combat between the Muslim and the Serbian armies in the enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the fall of Zepa, there was a break in the humanitarian aids; that's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And do you know, was aid always suspended when there was combat?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were combat operations carried out only by the Serbian forces, not from the inside. But there were frequent suspensions of humanitarian aid before the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Commander Delic here say that he was suspending further combat operations because of the people's need for humanitarian aid as well as the need of members of the Bosnian MUP? This is in line 3 of paragraph 3. If you don't want to, you don't have to answer. I can ask my next question, because I don't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should give the witness the opportunity to answer. He was just starting to answer your question, if he is able to do that. He didn't show any sign not to want to answer. I would like to receive the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how to phrase what I have to say. I've read the paragraph and this has nothing to do with anything. This is the first time that I'm seeing this document and the first time that I've heard about this. I don't know how to phrase what I have to say. I can just read out what it says in the document. I have no comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we've seen this again and again. The question that was asked was: "Did Commander Delic here say that he was suspending further combat operations because of the people's need for humanitarian aid," and so on and so forth. It's a question that's asking the witness simply to confirm what's on the document. How can the witness be expected to say anything more than, Yes, that's what I see. We have no problems, again, with General Tolimir asking substantive questions about what this witness's knowledge is about the topics in the document, but to simply ask him to confirm the plain language of the document doesn't get us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please, but focus on those areas the witness can testify about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hand out humanitarian aid in the place where you lived and stayed in the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my parents' village. I did hand out humanitarian aid there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And was humanitarian aid arriving during combat operations around the enclave and inside the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was suspended about a month before combat operations against the enclave began.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this with the leave of the Chamber, otherwise I would like to move on, because I don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not in the position to admit this document. The witness stated very clearly that he is not able to comment on the content of this document. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we now have D103. And while we are waiting, I would like to remind the witness of what he said on page 9866, line 13, of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said, and I quote, that you participate -- that you were a member of the army immediately before the fall of Zepa. The question was whether at that time all the men were defending the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all we were. We all went. Nobody called anybody. We all went to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we can see the document, D103. We can see that it was written by the War Presidency on the 15th of July, 1995, in Zepa. And at the time, the president of the War Presidency was Mehmed Hajric and he signed on this telegram. It is a telegram that he sent, and it says, and I quote; line 11 says: "All human and materiel resources have been made available for defence purposes. People with work obligation in the civilian protection have been made available to the 285th Brigade in Zepa." Further on, it says: "A widespread collection of good quality food for the soldiers, as well as blankets, foam padding, et cetera, has been organised. The morale of the soldiers is high." This is a report by the War Presidency that he sent to Sarajevo, to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the then-President Alija Izetbegovic. Now, my question is the following: This description of events that Hajric sends to Izetbegovic, can you tell us if it matches the situation in the field as you experienced it?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not even close, because there was a lot of fear. People had arrived who survived Kravica and Cerska and the break-through towards Tuzla and Srebrenica and they had come to Luke and Zepa and they were telling us about what the situation was like. It was far more dangerous than what this says. We were all at the lines because the attacks were very fierce and there was nobody in the village. You wouldn't dare be there the shelling was so heavy. I went one day to pick up some flour that I had and I saw cattle that had died around the houses, so I just grabbed the flour. I was so frightened. There was so much panic because everything was quiet, everything was deserted. So I tried to flee as fast as I could up to the line, up to where the lines were. The people were panicked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who the commander was at that line where you had returned from the village?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the leave of the Chamber, I would like to tender this document or I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have Exhibit D54 in e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for it, I will tell you that this is a document by Alija Izetbegovic to Mehmed Hajric dated the 19th of July, 1995. Alija Izetbegovic says the following, and now I will read paragraph 3 of the document sent by Izetbegovic to Hajric. Please have a look and I will read it. Alija says, and I quote: "My plan: Move out as many civilians as possible, all if possible. The troops stay on and continue to resist. We will do all to help you by supplying materiel and technical equipment, volunteers, and offensive action in your direction (I believe this is starting today). If we do not succeed in this, you try to push on, on those roads (you know which) but now without the burden of women and children who would in the meantime be taken out." Thank you. My question is the following: Was this what the soldiers of the BH army did? Did they do what Izetbegovic wanted them to do?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't demand anything of anyone, but I believe that they did try to find the free territory somehow. I ended up in Serbia and my goal had been to get to Macedonia, to free territory there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's see what you did. You brought your family to have them evacuated; can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was around the 25th. The 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you try to save your own life and when did you flee to Serbia across the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second or third day. I'm not sure about the days exactly but very soon after that. I ran into that school friend of mine. It was two or three days later. I believe I was captured on the 2nd, on the 2nd of August. I'm not sure about the date. It was very chaotic. It would be difficult to remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you decide to hand over your wife and your children to the Serbian army and to then continue on looking for free territory?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the Serbian army. I was hoping that that would be the ICRC and the UNHCR, that they would be transported in UNHCR trucks. They weren't lucky. They went through a lot of torture and a lot of fear. They were being transported by the Chetniks. And I set off hoping that I would reach Macedonia through Serbia unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did all the soldiers in the Zepa Brigade act as Alija Izetbegovic asked them? Did they send their women and children to the federation and did they stay on to fight or to try to get to the free territory any way they knew?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of combat are you talking about? A guard who was there, a guard in Serbia, told me that there were 15.000 soldiers in Zepa. He told me that in Serbia. You couldn't even think about doing something like that. All you thought about was getting to the free territory, getting away from that hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your -- this is the second time that you're telling us about something that somebody told you. Now, whether that was the truth or whether you saw a soldier from Serbia or captured him or killed him during the combat in Zepa. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Stublic. There was a reconnaissance group going and I had just arrived to replace the man who was before me. I asked, Who's up there? And the reply was, Krusevac. So he started walking. He thought that it was Krusevac in Serbia. And there's Krusev Do, which is a part of Luke municipality. At one point I saw that it was a Chetnik uniform; it was a uniform of the Yugoslav Army. And then I ran. He didn't shoot, and I was either scared or I didn't think I was skillful enough, but I'm certain of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were your positions facing Serbia or Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were facing the Chetniks in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the last stand on the Drina River, were you guarding -- were you defending from Serbia or were you defending from the Serbs in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in town on duty service one day without a weapon, because they had gone into Tegare village and they torched a blind woman in her house. This is quite an inaccessible terrain. Specialist army members might be able to get through there, and I was on guard duty there one day, unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you armed on that line where you were?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Stublic, yes. I took the rifle from the person that I replaced there. On the other hand, when I was in town for one day, I did not have a rifle. There were two of us and both of us did not have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P735 in e-court. P735, please. I'm interested in item 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's the agreement signed between the representatives of the military and the authorities in Zepa, commander of the UNPROFOR for Zepa, General Ratko Mladic, and commander of a brigade. I'm going to quote item number 8: "All population of military age in Zepa should be registered and accommodated in a holding centre which is to be under the control of the ICRC until the release of all captive VRS members and other Serbs who are in prisons in the territory controlled by the army under the command of Rasim Delic." So this is the agreement signed on the 24th of July, 1995. The agreement reached by the representatives of the VRS and the president of the Executive Board of the Zepa municipality Hamdija Torlak. My question is: Were all able-bodied persons in Zepa under obligation to register with the ICRC and were they supposed to be exchanged for the captured members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, UNPROFOR had a check-point at Stublic. They went to Zepa and left the population behind. Now, I see that some sort of agreement was indeed signed, but I have to say that if people remained there to wait and see what was going to happen to them, many of them would have perished. You have to know that many of them were tortured and went through many things. There was a private camp in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you among the able-bodied men in Zepa at the moment when this was signed by Hamdija Torlak?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For you, I would be able-bodied, because for you even people of 14 years of age and 80 years of age were able-bodied. Whoever was found to be there was able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you carry a weapon at Stublic and were you able to fire, or did you just carry it around for no particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, right, I carried it around for no particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Muslim army in Zepa turn their back on the agreement signed on the 24th of July? Did they actually betray the Serbian side after they had moved all the civilians to the territory of the federation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I had to cut off the microphone for a moment. Don't worry about that. We want to have your full answer on the record. And now, please, your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not renege. There were 14 people who were -- who, in the end, ended up in this some sort of a collection centre, which was actually a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You haven't really answered my question, but I'm moving on. Did you act contrary to this agreement because you left Zepa after your family left for the federation?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did manage to flee, but my journey was exceedingly difficult. Maybe this agreement could have been enforced if it was enforced in a humane way, but there were many people in Srebrenica with a similar agreement in their hand, in Srebrenica, and they were all killed. Also in 1992 in Bratunac, they signed a statement of loyalty and they would be taken away on the spot, imprisoned and killed. So this agreement is just an agreement, while acts are acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped you now, Mr. Tolimir, because you were overlapping again. Please pause between question and answer. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if I could just take us back a little bit. The -- there's a question at page 18, line 5, and it's about to disappear off our LiveNote. The answer at line 6, as I heard it, the question was: "Did you carry a weapon at Stublic and were you able to fire, or did you just carry it around for no particular purpose?" The answer, as I heard it interpreted, was: "Yeah, right, I carried it around for no particular purpose." I think my understanding is that was translating an idiomatic phrase, whatever it was, that is not reflected in the transcript as it appears, and I just want to make sure we've got an accurate answer. Because the way it reads on the cold transcript is different from what I understood the answer was. So before we go too much further afield from that, if we could have some clarification, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you know that every communication in the courtroom is taped and the transcript will be checked later. There are some parts missing, especially if the speakers are overlapping. That happens. You can't catch everything. And therefore I think we have now your concern on the screen. I heard different from what is to be read on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm only standing because it changes, potentially, the nature of the meaning of the answer. And that's the only reason I'm standing, to deal with it now, while we can, and not waste, you know, time, having to bring the witness back on redirect to deal with it. That's my only point. It's -- I'm not trying to quibble over minor words. It's something that I thought might potentially change the meaning of the answer, if you read it the way it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think your position is clear and we have that on the record. Now, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour - my greetings to everybody first - I'll be brief. I think that the interpreters interpreted the words of the witness correctly, as far as it was possible, because the word used in Serbian, "onako," means "without a particular purpose, without a particular goal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will request those who are responsible for checking the record to listen to the tapes in all languages and to clarify which is the right interpretation and recording. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you Mr. Thayer. Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Can we now have in e-court P736.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a decision by the War Presidency of Zepa dated the 27th of July, 1995. It is signed by Rajko Kosic [phoen], General Ratko Mladic, Hamdija Torlak, Mehmed Hajric, and Amir Imamovic, as members of the War Presidency. Are you aware of the fact that the members of the War Presidency made this decision on the 27th? And I quote the first paragraph: "All able-bodied men from 18 to 55 years of age shall surrender their weapons to the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska and to the representatives of UNPROFOR at the UNPROFOR base in Zepa. All able-bodied men shall be registered by the ICRC and shall be guarded by the forces of the VRS in the presence of UNPROFOR in Zepa until an agreement on exchange can be reached." Were you made aware of the fact that the War Presidency made such a decision on the 27th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about this. But Avdo Palic knows best how he was guarded by the Serbian army. He ended up dead in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You always answer my questions with a question of yours. So now I have to ask this: On a number of occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not correct. The witness didn't ask you anything. He stated that he doesn't know but perhaps another person. This is an answer, not a question. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on a number of occasions during this interrogation you said that some people were stopped at the very border-line when they were attempting to reach the territory of the federation, even mentioned a number; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard they were supposed to come out. I heard that when I was in the camp. It was a group of 70 people. They were somewhere near Olovo. Not a single one among them survived. I heard that four people went towards Gorazde. They have all disappeared as well, which means that they have been killed. Those four people from my village, I know them. I know one of them. His son was ill; he was 16 or 17 years old. He was transporting him on a horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you talking about the break-through from Srebrenica or are you talking about the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of break-through are you talking about? I don't know what you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows; I'm going to repeat it: Are you aware of the fact that on the 27th of July, 1995, the War Presidency made a decision that I just quoted? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the War Presidency requested the VRS to sign this decision and to take it to the Zepa mountain and read it out loud to the soldiers who were there?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that this decision was read out to the soldiers and that the soldiers refused to disarm in accordance with this decision?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Torlak testified here about this and he said that Mr. Mehmed Hajric personally took this decision to read it out to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about this decision or about reading out of this decision. But I believe that even if they read it out, nobody would be dare to go and surrender alive to the Chetniks. I'm absolutely sure about that. I now speak in my personal name. If I knew about this, I certainly wouldn't go to surrender. No, not alive. No, I'm one million per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on this very day, the 27th of July, when Mr. Hajric returned from the Zepa mountain and said that the soldiers refused to disarm, that the commander stopped the evacuation and the last convoy which also was carrying those people that you said were detained later on?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was not in Zepa at the time. It was Chetniks who were in Zepa at that time. They even captured members of UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was not allowed to walk around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember that yesterday during your testimony you said that some people were returned to the detention in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. 14 people from Luke were returned. I don't know about others, maybe there were more of them, but 14 people from Luke were in the camp in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know from where they were brought to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken off a convoy, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they reach the border with the federation before they were taken off the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that they were taken off the convoy because of the fact that the commander of the whole operation stopped the evacuation because the Muslims did not observe the agreement?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you took them off, but you took them off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just some clarification. This is the second question that's referred to the commander and just so we know to whom General Tolimir is referring in that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This relates to your question, Mr. Tolimir, page 23, line 22. Perhaps you can put the question to the witness and mention the name of the commander. It would help us better understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of the operation General Krstic ordered the evacuation to be stopped because the Muslims breached the agreement by refusing to disarm?

utterances.speaker: PW-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D111, page 25. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential exhibit and should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have to redact this part. And if you continue in that way, we should go into private session. Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, this concludes your examination in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in the courtroom, that you stayed such a long time and were able to provide us with your knowledge. Thank you again, and we wish you a safe journey back. And all the best for your future. And I'm so sorry that sometimes there were some confusions in the courtroom. That happens, and we have to make sure that we have a good record. Thank you very much again. We have to adjourn for our second break, and we will resume, to save time, quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. One quick issue. The last exhibit Mr. Thayer was dealing with, P00167, that list, it was an ICMP list, we didn't want to do it before the witness, but I've spoken to Mr. Gajic and he agreed that just for your knowledge that indicated -- or that record from those two people was surface remains. We didn't want you -- to suggest that it was a mass grave. Those two people were surface remains found in that greater Zepa area. Just before that bit gets ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next witness is ready. I really hope I can do this in much less than two hours. I really want to try to get her done tonight for many reasons, as I know the Court does. She suffered a lot and it may be difficult, but she's a pretty good witness and I hope to be able to get it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: She is a viva voce witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I had one exhibit but it's a picture of her husband and I don't think I'm going to show that to her. So I don't expect any exhibits. I'll just want her to tell her story. And I've told her that while we'll start at her home in 1992, to try to get to 1995 relatively quickly. So you will hear a little 1992 but we will -- we'll get to 1995 fairly quickly. And I hope to get her done hopefully within an hour, although it's really impossible. I may have to interrupt her at times, but I think we'll be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I read the witness summary, which is a very short one, carefully. So the Chamber is aware for which part of the whole story she is called. Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Hello to Mr. McCloskey and everybody else in the courtroom once again. I would just like to say for the record, where were these surface remains found? At what location? Was this in Zepa or was this at some other location? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the moment to deal with this problem. I understand this question but there will be a time we can deal with that. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Malagic. Welcome to the Tribunal, to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the information on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Perhaps the Court Usher can assist you with the earphones. I hope everything is fine. If there are problems, please let us know. Mr. McCloskey has questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And welcome back to the Tribunal. I think it's your first time back since the Krstic case in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us your year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In Peciste, Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Also in Peciste, Srebrenica municipality. Until I went to school, and then I spent four years in Zvornik in school. The rest of the time I spent there. Until 1978 or 1979 when I moved to Voljavica, Bratunac municipality, that's where we built a family home, my husband and I built a family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Peciste, is that a little village right next to the village of a now famous Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's 1 kilometre from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your family home, can you tell us, were you living in that home that you and your husband built right before the war started in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, you said the Bratunac municipality, can you tell us, you know, where?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a place that's 3 kilometres away from Bratunac. It's called Voljavica, and it's in Bratunac municipality. In the Drina Valley, along the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how close was your house to the Drina, the beautiful Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly metres, but there was one field that separated us. You walked down and then the Drina was right there, very close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did your husband do before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: He worked in the zinc mine. He was an accountant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us who lived in that family house with you before the war? You, your husband, any children?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, my husband and I and our three children: Adnan, Admir, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the third name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We lived there until May of 1992 when we had to leave our home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you say your three children's name again. They didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Elvir Malagic, born in 1973; Admir, born in 1979; and Adnan, born in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just -- you mentioned that you had to leave your -- that family home. And when did you leave the family home next to the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, 1992, at 7.30 in the evening. At 7.30 p.m., that's when we officially left the home. And we never returned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you leave the home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: We left because we were given an ultimatum. Voljavica village was in the same local commune as Pobrdje which is also in Bratunac municipality, and presidents of the local commune informed us of the situation and of what was happening those days. In the first days of May and the last days of April, we were no longer working. There was a lot of talk about leaving, a lot of talk about the war. Villages in Bratunac were being torched. And Bratunac was seized by soldiers; Novi Sad Corps members arrived in their APCs. The Sasa mine where we used to work was also occupied. There were Serbian soldiers there. I don't know to whom they belonged. So we stayed in the village and we couldn't leave. Bratunac was an option, but Serbian soldiers were there. There was the mine where, again, there were Serbian soldiers. There was the Drina, which was the border with Serbia, so we couldn't get across. And then we were given an ultimatum that we all had to go out in the streets, and this ultimatum was given by the leaders of the local commune. They told us that we could no longer live there, no longer stay there, and they said that we would be transported to another territory. People were afraid because of everything that we had seen until then and during those days. Some people decided to surrender and go out into the streets and others decided to flee into the nearby woods. I and my family was one of those who were in the woods because we didn't dare surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The leaders of the local commune, were those Serb leaders or Muslim leaders that gave this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned the Novi Sad Corps; is that an army corps from across the river in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So is it fair to say that you and the family you've described went out into the woods, as you've described, and you finally made your way to Srebrenica, and is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And were you able to find a roof to live under in Srebrenica beginning in -- sometime in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, 18 days after we had set off from home and when we reached Srebrenica through the woods, all the apartments had been abandoned. Srebrenica was deserted. Private homes had been torched, looted. There was nobody there. All the apartments were unlocked. They had all been searched. I don't know who did this, but all the apartments were unlocked. So you could enter into any apartment you wanted to without knowing whose place it was, and that's where we found accommodation for a few days because one of my sons was ill. He had a temperature, so we thought we would spend the night there. Three days later, I managed to talk to my brothers. I found out that they were alive. So we went to Potocari, to their family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have to move from Potocari back to Srebrenica at some point?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly explain that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In all of -- throughout 1992, we were in Potocari. There was a lot of shelling, and we stayed there as long as the house remained standing. And it was sort of habitable. But when it became inhabitable, we moved to Srebrenica. We found accommodation in a house, in a room, and that's where I was with my husband and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What caused your house, your brother's house, in Potocari to become not habitable?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: It was completely destroyed. It was destroyed by a larger calibre shell. It was completely destroyed. It had fallen down. It became uninhabitable. So they had to leave as well, my brothers, and come to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, and for the purpose of this trial and your testimony, I am going to now fast forward over those very difficult years of 1992, 1993, and 1994 and ask you, Were you living in Srebrenica in July 1995 with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us who was living in -- who you were living together with and their ages, so we now know the ages of your family, as of July 1995? As best you can recall.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived with my family, who I mentioned a moment ago, and my brothers lived in the same apartment with us. My older brother, Sadik Salihovic, was born in 1952. And Mirsad Salihovic, the younger one, was born in 1961. We were all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how old was your husband then?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: He was 45 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us how old your three sons each were in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The oldest one, Elvir Malagic, was 19 years old. Admir Malagic was 15 years old -- 15 years and five months old, and Amir [as interpreted] was 11 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July were you pregnant?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you eventually have a healthy baby daughter?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st of January, 1996, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And early in July of 1995, did you feel you had -- your family had to leave home again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain why.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the very end of June, and early July especially, there was complete chaos in Srebrenica among the people. Some people were trying to get across to the free territory. They self-organised into groups. They organised into arbitrary groups. There were all kinds of rumours about how Srebrenica was going to fall, how we all had to leave. People didn't know the real truth. They were uninformed. And there was talk among the people that the helicopters were taking people for further education [as interpreted]. Simple people, such as my family, my brothers and I, could tell that something was happening and that we would have to leave Srebrenica, that we would go somewhere. The only thing we didn't know, and we didn't believe that this would happen in the way that it happened in the end, that so many people would be killed. We thought that there would be a civilised fashion, that people would be transported in a civilised fashion. If necessary there would be an exchange of territories. I don't know what others were planning, but the simple folk didn't know about that. People were panicked. They were wondering where to go. People walked into ambushes, people got killed. Some people just went missing, and some actually managed to get across. Everybody tried to find their own way. My family, my brothers, my husband, my children, and I didn't go anywhere until we had to leave Srebrenica. I was in Potocari one day, and I can't remember what date it was. It was in early July, before the 11th. And we were walking, and about 3 kilometres from the firing range we could hear the first shells. All of a sudden my legs went numb because we hadn't had any shells in Srebrenica, at least not after UNPROFOR had entered. I was very frightened. We knew how things looked in 1992 and what combat operations looked like, so we were afraid. On the 10th of July, the 9th or the 10th of July, I believe it was, there were -- there was a lot of shelling. I don't know how many shells a day, but I know that shells fell on the hamlets. You know that there were thousands of people in Srebrenica, so none of these shells could miss. They had to kill or wound somebody. The hospital was full of wounded again. Again there was chaos. We didn't know where to go, we didn't know what to do, we didn't know what was going on, we had no information, and so on. It was on the 10th of July that we went to the UNPROFOR base again because people wanted to get some information on what was going on, and then the first UNPROFOR check-point was abandoned in Ljubisavici; it's up in Zeleni Jadar. UNPROFOR sent us back. The soldiers told us that nothing was happening and that we could go back to our apartments where we were in Srebrenica, so we did that and we spent the night there. Actually, nobody really slept that evening. We were trying to see what to do and where to go. We were talking amongst ourselves. The next morning, on the 11th of July, we were at home. We had packed some bread. We were unable to sleep. We just took some food for the children. My younger brother went to Potocari because we had a plot of land where we managed to sow some things, and he went to get us some potatoes and other food that was available there. We never managed to say good-bye. My brother, when he left the building, came back and said, You should all leave; the Serbian soldiers are at the former police station in Srebrenica. So we had to leave. And we all set off together. My father-in-law was with us and we started walking towards UNPROFOR. The former weaving plant in Srebrenica was the first UNPROFOR station. We passed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me interrupt you. And it may be self-explanatory, but why would the presence of Serb soldiers nearby cause you to want to leave your home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Because we didn't expect anything good from them. We remembered how we left our home in 1992 in Voljavica. There were killings that took place close to my house. People were taken away. People experienced suffering in Bratunac, and we saw this. My relatives had suffered in -- at the stadium in Bratunac. They were taken away from their families, and they're still missing to this day. In order to avoid getting into the same situation, we sought protection from UNPROFOR. There were so many shells that we didn't believe that we wouldn't get arrested, that we wouldn't be killed. The UNPROFOR soldiers were our last refuge, the Dutch soldiers. That's why we walked to their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that in Bratunac they were taken from their families. Can you describe what knowledge you had about that incident which, I believe, was in 1992 at Bratunac? What did you learn about that incident that caused you to be afraid in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early May 1992, my husband had two sisters. One was living in Bratunac and the other one 2 kilometres away towards Kravica; that's where she had a family home. Those days, my sister-in-law's house was torched and the whole Hrnici settlement. Some Serbian soldiers had arrived. They didn't arrest people, they just through some explosive devices. I don't know whether they were hand-held rocket launchers called Zoljas; I'm not an expert in this. But either way, the houses were on fire. You can't see the village from our village but in the evening the sky was on fire so you could see the houses burning. The next day, the next village you can see is Mihajlevici and then that village was torched. From the hill down to the road, they were torching everything. All the houses were on fire. Then the village of Suha, again, which we could see from our own home, was also torched; it was also in flames. They passed by our houses. They killed some men in Ledina, near Bjelovac, on the bridge between my house and my aunt's house, two men. I assume they started running from that vehicle, and they started chasing them for some 20 metres and then they shot them. They were killed next to our house. This was all in 1992 before the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there something that happened in Bratunac - you mentioned that people were taken away - something that happened in Bratunac around the soccer stadium that you were aware of in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe what you knew of that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: All men from Suha, from Mihajlevic, and from Bratunac, and the whole families, were taken to the stadium in Bratunac. My sister-in-law, her children, my other sister-in-law, they were all taken. And they told me about it, they survived it. There was another relative of mine, and his family as well, they were all taken to the stadium in Bratunac. They would separate them at the gate. They would let the women go and transport them towards Tuzla, while the men were taken to the Vuk Karadzic school. They were tortured there. Among others, one son of my aunt and his two sons were there in that school, Vuk Karadzic school. I know that for sure. When we left our home, we could watch the television. Those who know what kind of television the Serbian television is will know why we watched the other television, UTEL [phoen], while there was still electricity available. So I could see this relative of mine on the television. I don't know who put them on television, but he was telling what he experienced in that school in Bratunac. He is still alive and he can easily give a statement about it. His son was killed later on in Tuzla. They were exchanged in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to Srebrenica where you left off. It's July 11th and you've just made a decision; where do you go?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all left Srebrenica then. Everybody who was in town left Srebrenica town and went towards the UNPROFOR base. The UNPROFOR soldiers would not let us pass through towards Potocari at the beginning. When we were all there, gathered at that spot, it was a huge mass of people. They didn't know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. There's -- we know all know there's a couple of UNPROFOR bases. Where is this large gathering of people that you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: It's 1 kilometre from the centre of Srebrenica in the direction of Potocari. It's a former weaving plant. That was the first UNPROFOR base. It had a sign, UN, and you could still see it now. So that was our first stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And describe to us what happened there, what was going on now, again, as best as you can recall, but ...

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: My older brother, my husband, and my sons decided at that moment, with other able-bodied men, that they could reach Tuzla on foot. So they simply went towards the free territory. They were looking for a way out. They did not dare to go to Potocari. They told us women and children and the infirm to go towards Potocari, telling us that the UNPROFOR was going to protect us. They were not able to take the same route. My younger son was quite young but he was also quite tall and that was the reason that he went with them. They went towards the village of Susnjari. They separated from others at a gas station in Srebrenica. Not only them, but also many other people. That's when the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, to your knowledge, why was it that your husband didn't want to go to Potocari to seek protection from the UNPROFOR there? Why would he choose the woods instead?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I think that at that moment he was thinking the same thing that he was thinking in 1992 when we left our house: He didn't want to surrender to the Serbian authorities and Serbian soldiers. That's why we went into the woods in the first place. So then when we separated, that was also the reason. Many people went towards the woods. They did not trust that they would be protected in an adequate way. Because it was that first UNPROFOR check-point that let the Serbian soldiers through to enter Srebrenica. I'm not saying that they actually let them go, maybe they were simply powerless. But the fact is that people did not think that UNPROFOR was going to protect them in an adequate way. While we others, we could not go in the same way because it was a long way and we couldn't walk so far towards the free territory. That's why we, the others, went to seek protection from UNPROFOR, in their base. That was the only reason why they went that way through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you left off that you were around the UNPROFOR base in Srebrenica and you said that's when the shelling started. Do you remember roughly what time a day the shelling started at that Srebrenica UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't have a wristwatch. It was the 11th of July, in the morning. It was in the morning. But what time it was exactly, I'm not sure. It was morning. Because later on we spent maybe another two or three hours in that base, in the compound, and only after that we continued towards Potocari, when we were told that we could go there. So it may have been around 9.00 or 10.00. I didn't have a watch, so I cannot tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the shelling, where they hit.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Shells were landing all around. There was complete chaos and confusion. People screamed. Women with children sought shelter in the nearby buildings. Shells were landing all around. There were killed and wounded people. I was wounded by one such shell. That was a shell that fell a few metres away from me, within the UNPROFOR compound. My youngest son was with me and I thought that he was dead. My father-in-law was also with me and we all fell to the ground. When we got up, we realised that I was wounded. They were all very scared. Those who could seek shelter somewhere did that, but it was a complete chaos and confusion, so there were wounded people, lots of blood. There were so many people there that not a single shell could miss. As soon as a shell would land, it would land in the middle of a group of people. People were everywhere, in the street, on the pavement, around the buildings, on the gas station, on the road towards the former road assistance company. All able-bodied men decided to go into the woods and to go towards Tuzla to find salvation there, but I think that they were shelled along their way and there were some -- some of them were killed also along that way. They never managed to leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And, to be clear, from your family, you and your -- is it your 11-year-old son Adnan and your father-in-law stayed at the Srebrenica compound; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of your father-in-law and his approximate age?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Omer Malagic. He was around 70. He was born in 1926, so he was 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in my right-hand side of body. It was my right shoulder blade. I used to have a pull-over which was then full of blood. I used to keep it for a long time. It was full of shrapnels. Luckily none of them hit my head. It was just my shoulder blade and it was just a superficial wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You said you were there in Srebrenica for two or three hours. Where did you finally go and why?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that we have to stop at this point in time. There is a problem with the record. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that. We have to pause for a moment. We need a record, and it's not working. Now it's working again. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you left the Srebrenica UN compound after the shelling that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the UNPROFOR soldiers. We didn't understand their language but they showed us the way what their hands towards Potocari. At that moment we could hear the sound of aeroplanes. So they were showing us with their hands not to be afraid, that everything was going to be all right, and that we should go towards the Potocari military compound. And then, one by one, people went out of their base, and a huge mass of people went down the asphalt road all the way to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you with your son Adnan and your father-in-law along this asphalt road to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe that journey.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The journey was terrible. Shells followed us along the way, on both sides of the asphalt road. I can't tell you exactly the frequency, but they zigzagged from one side onto the other side. Some people were wounded by shrapnels. Whoever was wounded remained there. It was mainly women, children, and the infirm, and they couldn't help others. Some elderly people remained on the road because there was nobody available who could carry them. Nobody was strong enough for that. That's how we went the whole way to Potocari. It was maybe a kilometre and a half before Potocari that two UNPROFOR trucks caught up with us. One of them had the tarpaulin taken off and torn off and the truck was full of people. I recognised my son in one of trucks. I could see him, he saw me, and he waved towards me. He was there with a friend of his; they used to spend time together in Srebrenica. Those trucks passed us and went towards Potocari. That's when I saw him for the last time because I couldn't find hum in Potocari anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which son was that that you saw for the last time on that truck?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: It was my eldest, Elvir Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was the last time -- or where did you see your husband and your other son off that went to the woods?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: It was in front of the UNPROFOR gate in Srebrenica, close to the gas station. I don't know exactly how to describe it. That's where we parted. We didn't really have time to properly say good-bye. They went away because of the shelling. I don't know even today how it was that my eldest son in the end boarded the truck. I can only assume that. But after that, I haven't seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen your husband and the son that left with him, ever seen them alive again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you go when you finally get to Potocari that day, on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the afternoon, we arrived to Potocari. We went straight to the UNPROFOR base which was the former car battery factory. We came in front of the gate of the factory. They had already put yellow and red ribbons and there were UNPROFOR soldiers. They wouldn't let us pass. They told us that that place was full and that we couldn't go there, so we realised that the compounds itself was full, that the base was full, and that the rest of us simply couldn't go there. We had to stay in front of those ribbons in front of their gate. So I went back because I didn't want to be in the street on the asphalt. So we went instead into the nearby factory. There were some other factories nearby. And there were so many people looking for accommodation that we had to find some place. We were in the open air in the compound of the factory, in the zinc factory. Then there was also the factory called 11th of March, then there was the transport company of Srebrenica, so we simply went inside those compounds to seek shelter there. Other people did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is it fair to say that you and thousands of others spent the night in and around those factories and that that night was relatively quiet? And you've said before that people -- some people did feel safe that night; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when the sun comes up on the morning of the 12th, what happened? And, again, just briefly describe the main events that you recall that you've talked about before.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 12th of July -- well, first I have to say that in the evening on the 11th they were shelling the demarcation line, not around the people, but they were shelling the demarcation line. I was born there, so I know the area. We could hear bullets, explosive bullets, and sniper activity. I sat upright the whole night. I didn't get any sleep that night. And then the next morning on the 12th, they started from the nearby hills -- or, more precisely, from the village of Zogaze [phoen]. I know that place, that's Likari Pecic, I was born there. And we could see the houses being burned there. First they would torch the auxiliary buildings, so-called summer kitchens, barns, haystacks. Because, you know, people used to live in those houses. So we could see the houses burning and the people coming down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "they burned these places," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Serbian soldiers. The soldiers who were going down from house to house, torching the houses, until they arrived down and we could see them. They were going downhill, towards the compound of the transport company in Srebrenica. My brothers used to have a house there, but it had been destroyed earlier. So the soldiers arrived to a field right next to the people. There were some horses - I don't know whose horses they were - they tied the horses to a huge tree that was there and then they started shooting. They were shooting in the air, they were singing. They were having fun. They were making us scared. They also managed to scare the horses. And they would run around the tree. We could see that. You could see that in plain sight. We stayed where we were. We didn't go out of the compound. But the circle was getting tighter and tighter, because they also told the people who used to be in the houses and the hill that they should go down into the compound and that they were going to be evacuated. So the women from those houses would also arrive there and they would join us there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I apologise for interrupting. I would like to clarify one matter. The last question of Mr. McCloskey was: Who do you mean they burned the houses? And the answer was: Serbian soldiers. Are you referring to Serbian soldiers or Bosnian Serb soldiers? You use the term Serbian soldiers in your testimony frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I didn't express myself correctly. At the time, I didn't know whether they were Serbian soldiers in the meaning of Serbia or whether they were Bosnian Serb soldiers. They wore camouflage uniforms and they were soldiers and they were Serbs. Now, whether they were Serbian soldiers or the soldiers of Serbia, I didn't know that. When they arrived into the compound, you could see that there were many young men among them, so that's something that told me that they could be a regular army, because they were young. It's simply a conclusion of mine. Now, whether those people who were torching houses were Bosnian Serb soldiers or reserve soldiers, I wouldn't know. What I know is that they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us the other main events that happened on that day, the 12th of July, after the Serb soldiers, as you've described them, converged on the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around the part where I was, and many other women together with me, I was in one of the rooms in the zinc factory. My father-in-law he was in front of me. There were no doors, no windows, so we could see each other and communicate. They would come pass among us. They would interrogate us. Groups of them would arrive to ask us, Where are your men? Where are your soldiers? Where are your husbands? Where are your brothers? Where are your sons? Where are able-bodied men? Where did they go? It went on like this until the afternoon. They would go among us, walk among us look at us, ask questions. Some of them were - how should I put it? - you know, they were swearing. Some of them were swearing. They told us, Your Alija did all this to you. That's what they said. We were silent, of course. What else could we say? We didn't start any conversation or discussion unless you were asked something directly. A son of a colleague of mine was a bit of a naughty child and a neighbour of her came there to ask where her husband was. She said that he was wounded in 1993, that he was taken to Tuzla and further on to Germany, that he is now disabled. So they went away. So on that day, until the afternoon, they would take men in small groups and interrogate them. It was quite close to us, but we couldn't quite see what was going on.
